issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in acquitting the accused of the offence under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. on the ground that the number of participants was not proven to be five or more, thus failing to establish an unlawful assembly.

facts: The High Court found as a matter of fact that the prosecution had only proven the participation of four appellants in the crime beyond a reasonable doubt.
The presence and participation of the other eight accused persons were not proven.
The Supreme Court reviewed this finding of fact and found no valid reason to interfere with it.
law: An offence under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) requires the existence of an "unlawful assembly".
To constitute an unlawful assembly, the number of persons present and participating in the occurrence must be proven to be five or more.
If the number of participants is not proven to be at least five, the "common object" necessary for an unlawful assembly cannot be established.
application: The Supreme Court applied the law to the established facts.
Since the High Court had determined that the number of proven participants was only four (less than the required five), the essential condition for forming an unlawful assembly was not met.
Consequently, the prosecution failed to prove the existence of a common object necessary for a conviction under section 149 I.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was correct in acquitting the accused of the offence under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. The acquittal was justified because the prosecution failed to prove that five or more persons participated in the crime, which is a mandatory requirement to establish an unlawful assembly.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the High Court's finding of fact regarding the participation of the accused persons in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The High Court made a finding of fact regarding the participation of the accused persons.
It concluded that the participation of four appellants in the offense was proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
It also found that the presence and participation of eight other accused persons were not proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
law: Appeals to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution are a matter of discretion, and the Court is generally cautious about interfering with findings of fact made by lower courts.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's finding of fact concerning the participation of the accused.
The Court looked for a 'valid reason' to interfere with the High Court's conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no valid reason to interfere with the High Court's finding of fact and therefore upheld its determination regarding the participation of the four appellants and the acquittal of the others.

issue.issue_text: Whether the testimony of eyewitnesses can be held to be infirm and discarded solely on account of numerous infirmities, improvements, and variations in their statements.

facts: The case involved the testimony of four eyewitnesses (P.Ws 1, 2, 3, and C.W. 1).
The High Court had found that their testimony suffered from "numerous infirmities," including improvements and variations between their earlier and later statements.
All four of these eyewitnesses were injured during the incident.
The accused and the witnesses were known to each other and had a history of animosity.
law: A court's duty is to "remove the grain from the chaff," meaning it should sift through testimony to find the truth rather than discarding it entirely due to inconsistencies.
The quality of evidence is more important than the quantity or the number of witnesses.
The testimony of injured witnesses is highly credible because their presence at the scene of the crime cannot be doubted.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's reasoning that the testimony was infirm solely because of improvements and variations.
It reasoned that since the four eyewitnesses were injured during the incident, their presence at the time and place of the occurrence was undeniable.

The Court found that some variations and errors were natural, especially in the initial report (FIR) filed by a witness who had just sustained seven wounds and was taking other seriously injured people to the hospital.
The Court viewed the lack of a "parrot like stereotyped" account as a sign that the witnesses were not tutored, which strengthened their credibility.

It concluded that despite the noted improvements and variations, the core evidence from these natural and injured witnesses proved the presence and participation of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that eyewitness testimony cannot be held to be infirm and discarded solely on account of numerous infirmities, improvements, and variations. The court has a duty to separate the truth from the inconsistencies ('remove the grain from the chaff'), and in this case, the testimony was found to be credible because the witnesses were injured, making their presence at the scene undeniable.

cases.principle: Former statements of witnesses who are alive and testify in court are admissible under s. 157 of the Evidence Act to corroborate their testimony.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Common intention is a subjective question of fact that can be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case.
obiter: Former statements made by witnesses who are alive and depose in court are admissible under s. 157 of the Evidence Act to corroborate their testimony, even if such statements were erroneously called dying declarations.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, finding no valid reason to interfere with its finding of fact that only four appellants' participation was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the acquittal for the offence of forming an unlawful assembly under section 149 I.P.C. was correct, as the requisite five or more persons were not established. However, the court rejected the appellants' challenge to the eyewitness testimony, holding that infirmities or variations alone do not discredit witnesses and that it is the court's duty to separate truth from falsehood ("remove the grain from the chaff").
legal_tests_applied: When evaluating eyewitness testimony that suffers from infirmities, improvements, or variations, it is the duty of the Court to "remove the grain from the chaff" rather than discarding the testimony entirely.
In criminal prosecution, it is the quality of the evidence that counts, not the number of witnesses examined or the quantity of evidence adduced.
To establish an offence involving an unlawful assembly under section 149 I.P.C., the prosecution must prove the presence and participation of five or more persons.
The Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, will not interfere with a High Court's finding of fact unless a valid reason is presented.
why_appellant_lost: The Court found no valid reason to interfere with the High Court's finding of fact regarding the participation of the four appellants in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

The argument that eyewitness testimony should be discarded due to infirmities was rejected, as the court held that on that count alone, the testimony could not be held to be infirm and it is the court's duty to sift through the evidence.
The contention that not enough witnesses named in the FIR were examined was dismissed on the principle that the quality of evidence, not the quantity, is what matters.
The Court found the eyewitnesses to be the "best and natural witnesses" who knew the accused and had no reason to falsely implicate them.
why_respondent_won: The acquittal under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. was upheld because the prosecution failed to prove that the number of accused persons present and participating was five or more, which is a necessary condition for constituting an unlawful assembly.

The Supreme Court deferred to the High Court's finding of fact regarding the participation of the accused, stating, "We do not find valid reason to interfere with this finding of fact of the High Court."
policy_considerations: The judiciary has a duty to meticulously analyze evidence, even if it contains inconsistencies, to discern the truth, rather than taking the easier path of discarding it entirely. This ensures that justice is not defeated by minor imperfections in human testimony.
